title: Board Size
body:
**10x10 confirmed as viable.** Both players said size was generally right. Early game still has too much empty space (first contact at ~Round 7). 12x12 likely worse. Hex untested.
- **Remaining question**: Would 8x8 be better? Deferred to Stack D testing.
- **Status**: 10x10 is the baseline. Board size change tracked under Stack D scope.

title: Movement-Action Link
body:
**Unlinked works and is liked.** May be superseded by Unified AP system (Stack involving AP), which merges the concept entirely.
- **Status**: Unlinked is the baseline.

title: Skill Path Blockage
body: **Blocked by all pieces.** Both players confirmed.

title: Starting Piece Placement
body:
**Current placement is balanced.** Both players confirmed.
- **Note**: Becomes important again if piece count or board size changes. On 8x8 with fewer pieces, placement matters a lot more - will need re-evaluation.

title: First Player Advantage
body: **No strong advantage observed** in Playtest 1. Low priority. Re-evaluate only if first-player win rate becomes consistent across many games.

title: Rune Start Rate
body:
**Start with 6 Runes, +2 gain/turn, scaling +1 every 5 rounds. ACCEPTED.**
- Both players used skills from Round 1. Dead opening eliminated.
- Skill Slots became the action limiter in early game - as intended.
- Economy is fast enough without being overwhelming.
- **Status**: Accepted. Carry forward into all future stacks.

title: Shadow Shift Balance
body:
**Shadow Shift uses default Range 2** (not a special fixed cap).
- The prior "Range 3" fix was a misunderstanding - Shadow Shift uses the default Skill Range (2).
- **Status**: Resolved as Range 2 (default). Watch whether Range 2 feels limiting in practice.

title: Move Slots per Piece
body: **Each piece may only be moved once per Movement Phase.** Ruled mid-game Playtest 2.

title: Default Skill Range
body:
**Default Skill Range = 2.** Range 0 = self, Range 1 = adjacent, Range 2 = 2 tiles along Skill Path.
- Adjacent-while-injured edge case: minimum Range is 0 (self). A piece at Range 0 may always target itself.

title: Focus Strike / Blade Call Scope
body: **Focus Strike buffs the *next* skill used by any of your pieces that turn. Blade Call buffs any *one* Strike skill used by any of your pieces that turn (before or after).** Focus Strike must come first; Blade Call can be declared retroactively. Each Blade Call activation boosts exactly one Strike, then is spent.

title: Movement-via-Skills Damage
body: **Skills that move pieces do NOT deal damage.**

title: Blade Tempest Self-Affect
body: **Blade Tempest does NOT affect the caster.** Only the target takes 1 DMG; only pieces adjacent to the *target* are pushed.

title: Standard Attack Damage
body:
**Standard attacks deal 1 DMG instead of 2.**
- Playtest 3 (L2G1): first Champion kill **Round 11** (vs P2's R26). Both players Q2 "Felt right." Combat feel "Better / Much Better." Standoff dissolved.
- Risk that Guards become hard to remove - **not observed**. First Guard kill R10. Guards behaved as screens rather than damage sponges.
- **Status**: Accepted into baseline. See `mechanics-evaluated.md`.

title: Standoff / No-Man's-Land Problem
body:
**The standard attack nerf (OQ-37) dissolved the standoff in Playtest 3.**
- Both players: "Much less standoff" / "Not reluctant to move forward." Forward movement active from early rounds.
- **Confirms primary research finding**: lower entry risk + sente design dissolves standoff.
- **Status**: Confirmed resolved by Stack A Game 1. Sente design (Stack F) is no longer urgent. Watch for re-emergence with two experienced players.

title: Rune Cap
body:
`[System: Resource Economy] [Affects: Skill System]`
**No hoarding observed in Playtest 3** - neither player accumulated unspent Runes meaningfully. Both players said "always wanted more / balanced." Confirms G2 (encourage spending via attractiveness) is working.
- **Status**: Closed. No cap needed.

title: Injured Penalty Severity
body:
- Speed penalty is Guard-only. The only Champion/King Injured effect is Skill Range -1 (affects Range 2+ skills only).
- **P3 blocker**: Lance Thrust + Injured ambiguity cost Elias a turn at R22. Blocked severity evaluation.
- **Resolution (Session 18)**: Baseline already contains the complete ruling. Range-1 is a modifier from default Range 2, so an Injured piece using Lance Thrust has effective Range 0 (self only) - it cannot fire. This is derivable from `baseline-sections.typ` lines covering Range modifiers and the Injured Range penalty.
- **Remaining watch**: The rule requires chaining three lines of text - not explicit at the table. OQ-54 tracks whether "Range-1" language causes confusion in practice.
- **Status**: Closed. Severity is evaluatable; watch OQ-54 for wording clarity.

title: Economy Skills as Skill Slots
body:
- With only 2 skill slots per Champion, equipping an economy skill makes that piece a "one-trick pony" - sacrifices combat versatility entirely.
- **Session 8 verdict**: Closed permanently. 2-slot scarcity makes this unworkable. The core idea (ultra-defense → late-game payoff strategy) is interesting as a post-v1 expansion variant, not a core system change.

title: Performance-Based Rune Gain
body:
`[System: Resource Economy] [Affects: Combat, Progression]`
- Performance-based income forces players toward whichever strategy earns Runes fastest, constraining creative expression. Auto-economy is strategy-neutral. The combo bonus is the correct lever: it rewards *cleverness of execution*, not *which action you performed*.
- **Status**: Closed. Not revisiting.

title: Health System (3 HP)
body:
**3 HP for Champions/King was the proposed test, but it has been scrapped before testing.**
- Reason: 3 HP would make the game even longer (first kill was already at R26 with 2 HP). Guards at 2 HP with Champions at 3 HP creates an artificial rank.
- The underlying problem (combat too coarse, Injured state bypassed by standard attacks) was solved by OQ-37 (1 DMG standard attack) instead.
- **Status**: Scrapped.

title: Terrain System
body: **Confirmed as overhead complexity.** Removed in A+ direction. Reversible - can return as "map variant" expansion if missed.

title: Restricted vs. Free Movement
body:
**Free pathing is the baseline.** Restricting movement to straight-line-only would punish Guards (Speed 2 in a straight line is terrible for navigation) and is meaningless for Champions (Speed 1). Dissolves entirely if hex grid is adopted.
- **Status**: Parked. Only revisit if Move skills feel weak AND hex is not adopted.

title: CR-Style Draft Picks
body:
`[System: Skill Drafting]`
- Restricts free strategy picking - with a small catalogue, counter-picking leads to "correct" picks that reduce variety. Only relevant with a much larger catalogue (20+ skills).
- **Status**: Parked. Variant/expansion material.

title: Ban Phase in Skill Draft
body:
`[System: Skill Drafting]`
- From an older game version with unique Champions that had fixed skills. The current system (shared skills, free assignment) makes banning less meaningful. Needs 20+ skills AND a different draft model to be viable.
- **Status**: Parked.

title: Starting Player Decision
body:
`[System: Turn Structure]`
- No first-player advantage observed in 2 playtests. If it ever surfaces over many games, the fix is Go-style komi (P1 starts with fewer Runes), not a bidding war.
- **Status**: Parked. Only revisit if consistent first-player win rate observed across many games.

title: Bodyguard Rule
body:
**Hypothesis**: Bodyguard triggers more frequently with adjacent-to-defender-only rule.
- Original test artefact: previously at `docs/test-scenarios/stack-b-guards/stack-b-bodyguard-fix.typ` - *deleted Session 23*. Stack B was withdrawn Session 22 (defender-only adjacency change is no longer the proposed solution). The original rule sheet is no longer kept on disk; see the Withdrawn row in `docs/mechanics-log/mechanics-evaluated.md` for the historical record.
- **P2 update**: Bodyguard triggered 2x under baseline adjacency rule.
- **P3 update (Session 15)**: Bodyguard organically activated under Stack A nerf - standoff dissolved was the actual cause.
- **P4 update (`docs/research/playtest-4-analysis.md`)**: 0 triggers (regression). Both players: "didn't trigger / not so many move-attacks / even less kills." **Confirms Bodyguard tracks standoff state, not the rule.** When mid-game stalling returned (Armor-driven), Move-attack volume dropped, and Bodyguard had nothing to intercept. OQ-21 cannot be evaluated cleanly while standoff/stalling is a moving variable.
- **Attacker movement on intercept**: RULED - attacker moves 1 tile toward target (stops before Guard). Applied to baseline.
- **Stack B withdrawn (Session 22)**: Defender-only adjacency is unlikely to be the right fix even if Bodyguard remains broken post-Stack-H. Different solutions (e.g. simplify/remove Bodyguard per the Framing-B watch-flag below) would be on the table. The OQ itself stays open; the originally proposed stack does not.
- **Re-entry trigger**: re-evaluate Bodyguard *behaviour* after Stack H. If Armor trim reduces stalling and Move-Attacks return, Bodyguard becomes triggerable again - only then is the rule itself testable. If a fix is needed at that point, draft a new stack rather than reviving Stack B.
- **Framing-B watch-flag (added Session 20, Q-C2 finding)**: Bodyguard is the most chess-coded mechanic in the chassis - confirmed combo-irrelevant in P3 (Mario's usage was trade-up defensive screening, not combo-positioning). Not actionable today, but if a future stack proposes simplifying/removing Bodyguard for chassis-volume reasons, Framing B (ADR-004) is one of the supporting arguments. See Q-C2 in `docs/research/high-concept-open-questions.md`.

- **Engine implementation (Session 31, 2026-06-23)**: The dual-adjacency Bodyguard rule (canonical rules-sheet text: "Guard intercepts only if it sits adjacent to BOTH the tile immediately before the target along the attack path AND the defending piece") is implemented in `crates/core_engine/src/game_logic/{action,generator,make_unmake}.rs`. Attacker physically advances to the penultimate tile on a Move-Attack (speed-2 Guards: zig-zag paths produce distinct legal actions with different Bodyguard sets; speed-1: approach == src). The OQ itself remains open: the question is whether this rule is the right *design*, not whether it is wired correctly. Re-evaluate post-Stack-H per the existing re-entry trigger.

title: Steal Balance
body:
**Mode A** (opponent at 0 Money): Steal is a normal-range Strike skill (1 damage, no theft effect). Not dominant.
**Mode B** (opponent has Money): cheap damage + opponent disabling. Tempo weapon. Disable value time-dependent: early-game high impact, late-game low impact.
- **P4 evidence**: Elias Q9 *"Steal again feels very strong in some situations"* + must-pick. Niko's R26-R28 winning loop = Tempest + Steal + Focus. Niko Q15 favourite: *"stealing money to prevent skills next turn"* - celebrating Mode B. Elias R8 actively neutralised Niko's Steal champ early.
- **Session 25 - absorbed into Stack M**: Steal cost 3→4 for both Modes. Targets Money economy faucet rebalance and Mode B dominance simultaneously. Rollback path: if combo widening + cost increase together kill cleverness ("pure aggression dominates"), roll back combo widening OR Steal cost increase depending on which axis feels off (per Stack M routing).
- **Re-entry trigger**: Stack M playtest result. If Steal still must-pick at cost 4, escalate to cost 5 or a structural rework. If Steal becomes ignored, dose was too high.

- **P6 update (2026-07-09, first digital Stack M playtest - `essay-playtest-6-analysis`)**: Cost 4 "finally felt fair" (designer). Not ignored, not must-pick. No escalation to cost 5 needed. Overshadowed only by Tempest (same cost) due to combo-widening impact - Tempest is a watch-flag, not a Steal problem. **Trending toward resolved on the accepted-direction.**

title: Multi-Champion Combo Bonus
body:
**+1 damage on the second+ Strike hit when 2+ different Champions target the same enemy this turn.**
- Buff skills targeting your own pieces do NOT count.
- Charge stacks with combo bonus (separate effects).
- Strike-only for Stack A G2 (decided Session 16). Cross-category scope reconsidered after G2 data.
- **P4 evidence (`docs/research/playtest-4-analysis.md`)**:
  - Elias R11 margin "1. ever combo!!" - first multi-Champion combo across 4 playtests (behavioural).
  - Niko's R26-R28 = 3 consecutive Strike+Strike kill rounds = winning loop.
  - 5 combo bonus activations on Elias's sheet; Niko 2/2 attempt-success.
- **Session 22 reframe (designer pushback)**: the "weak in feel" reading from the original analysis was wrong. The bonus is **by design** a few-times-a-game payoff, not an every-turn activation - a Q3 "Somewhat / Bit of both" reading is exactly right for that design intent. The lever is **scope**, not **strength**.
  - Cross-category crowd-out is a real consequence of Strike-only scope, not a bonus-strength problem.
  - Elias's late-game offensive lockout (#6) - *"i did not have any other attack champs left"* - is a scope-reachability problem too: the bonus was structurally locked away when his Strike-equipped Champs died. Single-Champion offense doesn't trigger the target counter.
- **Session 25 - target-counter widening absorbed into Stack M**: Stack M widens the *target counter* to also tick on **movement-causing skills** that move the target (Tempest push, Hook pull, Blast push, Shove, Swap when relocating enemy). Move-Attacks still excluded. Self-movement (Dash, Retreat) excluded.
- **Session 26 - bonus-damage scope expanded inside Stack M**: bonus damage now applies to *any* skill - Strike *or* movement-causing - that affects a target with counter > 0, not only to Strike hits. Movement skills become a damage vector once a target is counter-loaded. Designer rationale: this unlocks damage strategies without Strike skills and gives more utility/strategic options. Counter-tick rules unchanged (still requires new Champion + Strike-or-movement). This is a substantive expansion of OQ-38's scope beyond the originally drafted Stack M dose. Watch flag: if dual-effect skills (Tempest, Hook) feel overwhelmingly dominant, first rollback is "movement skills tick counter but only Strike skills deal bonus damage" (drafted in Stack M Facilitator Notes routing).
- **Stack A G3 attacker-counter - DEFERRED post-Stack-M**: The *attacker counter* (same Champion hits different targets → bonus) is NOT in Stack M. Remains as Stack A G3 candidate if Stack M's combo widening does NOT auto-resolve the exchange-pit pattern (OQ-58). Session 25 narrowing note in `docs/backpocket.md`: attacker counter felt too generous on reflection - narrow at design time when Stack A G3 is drafted.
- **Teaching cost flag (G4 / OQ-60)**: Stack M's widening keeps a single counter (no second parallel counter yet); cognitive-load increase is modest. Stack A G3's dual-counter would still need tokens/board-side trackers.
- **Status**: G2 single-counter Strike-only is in baseline. Stack M widens target counter to movement-causing skills. Stack A G3 (attacker counter) deferred post-M.

- **P6 update (2026-07-09 - `essay-playtest-6-analysis`)**: **Combo widening ACCEPTED (designer call).** "Finally very usable… very versatile"; not single-dominant (cheap Hook+Lance nearly beat a combo-maximiser). 8/9/12 counter-loaded skill plies across 3 games - actively two-sided. NOTE: a separate **engine bug** (bonus damage mis-gated on combo_tick, so the SAME Champion re-striking a counter-loaded target drops the +counter bonus; cost the designer a game) does NOT contaminate this design verdict - see next_steps bug B1. **Tempest watch-flag retained** for future playtests.

title: Mid-Game Stickiness / "Exchange Pit"
body:
`[System: Combat / Positioning] [Affects: Mid-game pacing, parallel-puzzle texture]`
**Once a melee exchange starts, basically all the action happens there until the end of the game. Pieces get taken one-by-one in a single localised cluster; outside the cluster nothing happens.**
- **P4 evidence**: Elias D-note: *"once an exchange starts, basically all the action happens there until the end of the game."* The R15-R21 Armor cluster + R22-R28 kill loop both happened in a single board region.
- **Designer note (Session 22)**: distinct from "both players don't know what to do" - that's an early-game positioning + post-exchange endgame conversion problem. Exchange-pit is specifically the mid-game pattern *during* the cluster.
- **Distinct from OQ-11 (Armor volume)**: Even with Armor trimmed (Stack H), the *positional* convergence of all action into one pit is its own pattern. Armor stalling fills downtime; exchange-pit constrains where action happens.
- **Distinct from OQ-19 (endgame acceleration)**: First Champion kill timing is healthy (R13). The problem is not "kills come too late" - it is "all kills happen in the same place, sequentially, with no parallel pressure."
- **Hypothesised lever (Session 22)**: dual-counter combo bonus (see OQ-38 Stack A G3 plan). The proposed **attacker counter** rewards a single Champion hitting *different* targets in one turn, structurally encouraging multi-front pressure rather than one-pit convergence.
- **Other candidate levers** (no Justification Rule writeup yet - flag only):
  - Sente / threat skills (Stack F territory) that create incentive to defend a *different* part of the board.
  - Centre-attractor mechanic (overlap with OQ-52 - central tile attractors could split the action geographically).
- **Re-entry trigger**: post-Stack-H. If chassis trim doesn't reduce exchange-pit pattern, dual-counter combo (Stack A G3) is the targeted fix. If exchange-pit dissolves under Stack H alone, Q-C1 was masking it and dual-counter may not be needed.
- **Connected to**: OQ-38 (combo scope widening); OQ-52 (centre attractor); OQ-11 (chassis volume - masking variable).

- **P6 update (2026-07-09 - `essay-playtest-6-analysis`)**: P4 single-pit convergence did NOT reappear. BUT a distinct mid-game **"first-mover-loses" tempo pattern** surfaced: whoever breaks a standoff loses a piece on the trade, so both wait for economy to rebuild ("wait so I have money again to attack"). Designer note: this is a *tempo/incentive* problem, **NOT a draw-condition problem** (players wanted a give-up button, never a draw). Candidate levers: reduce first-mover trade disadvantage, or add tempo pressure. Do NOT route to draw conditions. Related: Dorian wants >2 moves per Move Phase.

- **Session 45 update (2026-07-11 - Stack N staged)**: the first-mover-loses tempo pattern was diagnosed to a **root cause**: ranged skill-kills are *non-reciprocal* (unlike chess capture, the attacker pays no positional price - kills from distance, victim loses piece + anchor, attacker stays out of range). Staged **stack-n ("Lethality & Standoff Pass")** as the fix: (1) Focus cost 1→2, (2) max 1 move-attack/turn, (3) **strike-moves-caster** (casting a Strike moves the caster 1 tile toward the target - restores positional cost / reciprocity). Held in reserve: **Candidate X** (`bp-forward-guard-partial-skill-immunity`) - forward Guards partially skill-immune, deploy only if Guards still evaporate. oq-86 (loser-rebate) parked as fallback. Explicitly NOT routed to draw conditions.

title: Opening + Endgame "Don't Know What To Do" Pattern
body:
`[System: Whole-game / Positioning / Strategic clarity]`
**Two distinct dead-air pockets in the same game: (a) early-game positioning (where to put pieces, no combat reachable yet); (b) post-mid-game-exchange endgame (the cluster is over, the game isn't, and neither player has a clear plan to convert the resulting position into a win).**
- **P4 evidence**: Elias D-note: *"there were a lot of turns where we both didn't really know what to do."* Designer's Session 22 clarification: this happens specifically (a) at game start before pieces meet and (b) after the central exchange ends, not generically across the whole game.
- **Distinct from OQ-58 (exchange-pit)**: exchange-pit is "all the action lives in one place during mid-game." This OQ is "before and after the exchange there is no clear strategic gradient."
- **Distinct from OQ-11 (Armor)**: Armor stalling is *what players do when they have nothing better to do.* This OQ is the underlying *why nothing better is available* - the strategic gradient is flat in those windows.
- **Sub-problem 59a - Opening incentives skew chassis-ward**: at game start, no Strike skills firing (pieces too far apart for Range 2). Only Defense + occasional Move-Attack. Move skills sit idle despite being equipped. Players move chassis-level (whole pieces forward) rather than skill-level. **Designer note (Session 22)**: *"there are no strike skills at the start ONLY defense (or sometimes move-attacks)."*
- **Sub-problem 59b - Endgame conversion gap**: when the central exchange ends, the resulting position should *suggest* a winning plan. P4: it didn't. Both players sat stumped on how to convert.
- **Candidate levers (no Justification Rule writeups yet - flag only)**:
  - For 59a: Move skill repricing in opening; OQ-1b 8×8 board (Stack K G1) reduces opening distance; combo-bonus widening to include Move skills (OQ-38) - gives Move-into-Strike offensive value early.
  - For 59b: King-as-real-target (overlaps OQ-53); cascade trigger / threat skills (Stack F); central attractor (OQ-52).
- **Re-entry trigger**: re-evaluate after Stack H + Stack A G3 + Stack K. The dead-air windows may shrink as chassis volume drops and combo grammar widens. If they persist, dedicated stack(s).
- **Connected to**: OQ-52 (centre attractor); OQ-53 (King role); OQ-1b (8×8); OQ-38 (combo scope); OQ-58 (exchange-pit - pairs with this).

title: Two-Pole Parallel Design
body:
`[System: Project methodology / Game shape]`
**Should the project carry both versions forward indefinitely as game *modes*, or is Pole B (per-turn-draft) an experiment that *replaces* Pole A (pre-game-draft) if it lands?**
- **Origin**: Session 23 discussion - see `docs/research/path-y-defense-redesign.md`. User crystallised two parallel game versions rather than continuing to tweak variables inside a single rule set.
- **Pole A** = pre-game-draft (current game). **Pole B** = per-turn-draft (skills added during play; 12-equipped cap; shared action slots; no Money activation gate).
- **P5 result (2026-06-21, Elias P1 vs Jonathan P2, digital, 15 rounds)** - full notes: `playtest-results/elias-vs-jonathan-pole-b-digital-2026-06/notes.md`. Three structural problems surfaced:
  1. **Armor 3 still felt mandatory** - Jonathan flagged unprompted; cross-pole confirmation of OQ-11.
  2. **Pure-reaction play** - board state shifted too dramatically per turn for multi-turn planning. Breaks Principle 4.
  3. **Felt PI broke** - combinatorial breadth made formal-PI invisible; players reported losing the "perfect information" feel. (Distinct from OQ-62 which is about Pole A sequential draft determinism - see new OQ-64.)
  - Length dropped (15 rounds vs P4's 28-29) but the short game lacked "overarching tactic" feel - short *because* nobody planned, not short *and* satisfying.
- **Resolution (Session 25)**: **Pole A continues as the Active track.** Pole B (consumable-skills variant) is paused. Other Pole B variants in `docs/backpocket.md` (permanently-equipped, activation-cap, resource-cost-on-activation) remain alive as future experiments if the Pole A track stalls again. This is NOT "Pole A replaces Pole B" - Pole B is paused at this variant; the underlying *direction* (in-game skill acquisition) may return.
- **→ Move to OPEN_QUESTIONS_ARCHIVE.md next archive pass.** OQ stays alive briefly as load-bearing context for the Session 25 → 26 transition.
- **Connected to**: OQ-62 (Pole A draft information - still live, scope unchanged); OQ-63 (cross-pole fixing - resolved on first encounter, see below); OQ-11 (Armor - cross-pole confirmed); OQ-64 (felt-PI vs formal-PI - opened from P5); OQ-65 (onboarding via pre-made loadouts - opened from P5); OQ-66 (game length target - opened from P5).

title: Cross-Pole Fixing Methodology
body:
`[System: Project methodology]`
**When a problem (e.g. Armor's role) exists in both poles, do we run the fix in each pole separately, or once and carry across?**
- **User lean (Session 23)**: *"its cleaner if we have to run it twice, once per pole, but i also say that it could be confusng if we do not clearly seperate both poles from one another."* Two-pole-twice is the default lean, with confusion as the explicit risk.
- **First encounter (Session 25)**: P5 confirmed Armor 3 feels mandatory in Pole B too (cross-pole confirmation of OQ-11). With Pole B now paused (OQ-61 resolution), the methodology question collapses to a simpler shape: Stack H runs in Pole A only. If Pole B is ever revived, Stack H (or its successor) runs again there. **Carry-forward is per-pole-revival, not once-and-carry.** Confirms the original lean without forcing an actual two-pole-twice run.
- **→ Move to OPEN_QUESTIONS_ARCHIVE.md next archive pass.**
- **Connected to**: OQ-61 (two-pole framing); OQ-11 (Armor - first shared-fix surface).

title: Felt PI vs Formal PI
body:
`[System: Whole-game / Information / Cognitive load]`
**When a turn has too many possible picks × actions × interactions, does the *feeling* of perfect information break down even though formal PI holds?**
- **Origin**: P5 (Pole B, Elias vs Jonathan) - both players reported that the breadth of pick × action × skill-interaction options per turn made the game feel like incomplete information, despite all state being technically visible. Designer verbatim: *"es gab halt so viele möglichkeiten ... sodass man nicht mehr das gefühl von 'perfekter information' hatte."*
- **Why it matters**: Perfect Information is a hard constraint (`design-principles.md`). If a design produces formal-PI but loses felt-PI, it has lost the *thing PI was supposed to deliver* - the ability to plan from a fully readable board. Felt-PI failure breaks Principle 4 (cleverness > attrition) by making multi-turn planning impossible.
- **Distinct from OQ-62**: OQ-62 is about *informational asymmetry* introduced by sequential draft (knowing what opponent already picked before you commit). OQ-64 is about *informational overload* breaking PI even when nothing is hidden. Same axis (information), different failure mode (asymmetry vs overload).
- **Distinct from OQ-60 (cognitive load)**: OQ-60 asks "is per-turn thinking proportional to payoff?" OQ-64 asks "does the *visible* state space fit in a player's head well enough to read?" Cognitive load can be high while felt-PI holds (chess endgames); felt-PI can break while load is medium (Pole B P5).
- **Design constraint flagged**: any future system addition needs a felt-PI smell-test. "Can a player look at the board and read what's possible in the next 1-2 turns without consulting external state?"
- **Re-entry trigger**: surfaces in any future stack where per-turn option space expands sharply (combo widening, skill catalogue expansion, Pole B revival, AP system).
- **Connected to**: OQ-60 (cognitive load); OQ-56 (Problem C2 - skill identity volume); OQ-62 (Pole A draft determinism); Principle 4 (cleverness > attrition); hard constraint "Perfect Information."

- **P6 update (2026-07-09 - `essay-playtest-6-analysis`)**: No felt-PI collapse reported. BUT move-phase branching factor hit avg 39-49 / **max 392-420** (from telemetry legal_count). Watch: high move-phase option count is the most likely felt-PI stressor if it grows.

title: Pre-Made Loadouts for New Players
body:
`[System: Onboarding / Draft / Pole A revival track]`
**Should new players skip the pre-game draft entirely and play with a curated starter loadout, with drafting unlocked only for experienced players?**
- **Origin**: P5 - Pole B was partly motivated by "first-game players can't evaluate skills during draft" (OQ-56 Problem A). P5 confirmed Pole B *replaced* that problem with a worse one (felt-PI breakdown, OQ-64). Designer's call: solve OQ-56 Problem A inside Pole A directly, via **pre-made loadouts**. Verbatim: *"unerfahrene spieler nutzen pre-made picks."*
- **Pre-thought design**: 2-3 curated starter loadouts per side (e.g. "Aggro", "Defense", "Combo-focused"). New players pick a loadout, not individual skills. Experienced players continue with the full draft. Removes the entire draft cognitive load for new players without removing strategic depth from the game itself.
- **Justification (per Rule)**: Fixes OQ-56 Problem A (draft entry complexity) without introducing the felt-PI / pure-reaction problems Pole B surfaced. Game-feel improvement: new players get a comprehensible first game; experienced players keep the full draft experience.
- **Risks to monitor**:
  - Loadout selection becomes its own draft determinism problem if presented sequentially (use simultaneous reveal - connects to OQ-62).
  - Curated loadouts may bias new players toward a specific play style, hiding strategic variety.
  - "Mandatory upkeep" / must-pick skills (Armor, Steal, Focus) become more visible if they appear in every loadout - exposes a different chassis-volume problem.
- **Re-entry trigger**: this is now a candidate Active stack for Pole A revival (alongside OQ-66).
- **Connected to**: OQ-56 (draft entry complexity - direct fix for Problem A); OQ-62 (simultaneous-reveal could pair with loadout selection); OQ-66 (game length - short games make a "wrong" loadout less punishing).

- **Session 33 decision**: Pre-made loadout mode will exist as a **pre-game choice alongside the default custom draft**. Players pick at match start: "custom draft" (default, experienced players) OR "pre-made loadout" (new players).
  - **Mirror match**: when pre-made mode is picked, **both players play with the same loadout** so the training-wheels track has perfect fairness on the loadout axis.
  - **Curated progression, not playstyle archetypes**: the curated loadouts will be framed as "First game / Second game / Third game" (escalating complexity) rather than "Aggro / Defense / Combo" (playstyle bias). Reasoning: a playstyle frame either biases the new player toward one approach or forces them to evaluate playstyles before they have a game model - both of which OQ-65 was meant to avoid. Progression framing implicitly teaches: each loadout introduces a few more interacting skills than the previous.
  - **The current pre-made loadouts are bad and will not be shipped.** New loadouts to be designed by the user when implementation lands.
- **Status stays open** until: (a) the new tutorial loadouts are designed, AND (b) the pre-game mode picker UI is built. Decision is locked; execution is pending.

Sequential draft inside pre-made mode is moot anyway because both players use the same loadout.

title: Game Length Target
body:
`[System: Whole-game pacing / Principle 6]`
**Can game length be drastically reduced to a 30-60 minute target without sacrificing the "overarching tactic" feel?**
- **Origin**: P5 - designer verbatim: *"es ist gut, wenn das game schnell vorbei geht, aber man will trotzdem noch das feeling haben von 'ich habe eine overarching taktik und will diese anwenden um zu gewinnen'. ich glaube wirklich der nächste schritt ist erstmal bei pole a zu bleiben und sich darauf zu fokussieren ... die länge vom spiel drastisch zu verringern (auf so 30-60 minuten maybe)."* P5 itself ran 15 rounds (fast) but felt empty - short + reactive is bad. Target: short + with overarching tactic.
- **Why it matters**: Principle 6 (game length is itself a form of attrition). P4 ran 2h30; reducing to 30-60 min unlocks more playtests per session, lower onboarding friction, and meets the actual playability bar for first-time players.
- **Stack M operationalization (Session 25)**: Six bundled changes target game length on multiple compounding axes simultaneously (per the 12-economy map): board 8×8 (tile economy / combinatorics), Armor cap 2 (chassis volume), Injured-no-penalty (damage-vs-heal asymmetry), no draws (single-climax shape), Steal cost 4 (Money faucet rebalance), combo widening (engagement more attractive than stalling). Each lever maps to a specific compounding curve identified in `docs/research/game-economy-map.md`.
- **Risks (still apply)**:
  - Cutting too fast removes the multi-turn-planning window the core fantasy lives in.
  - "Short *because* nobody planned" is the P5 failure mode - guard against it.
  - Player skill asymmetry feels worse in short games (less time for newer player to learn / recover).
- **Re-entry trigger**: Stack M playtest result. If target met but feel broken → roll back the offending axis per Stack M routing. If target not met but no stalling → Stack K piece reduction is the next isolation lever.
- **Connected to**: Principle 6 (game length as attrition); Principle 8 (single climax); OQ-11 (Armor - absorbed); OQ-27 (Stack K - piece count, queued post-M); OQ-1b (Stack D - 8×8 absorbed); OQ-65 (pre-made loadouts - sequenced post-M).

- **P6 update (2026-07-09 - `essay-playtest-6-analysis`)**: Length rated 3/3 (just right); 17-26 rounds. Overarching-tactic feel present (favourite moment = "finding clever full-turn moves in a position"). Caveat: sandbox feature inflates wall-clock but is a *wanted* feature, not a length regression. Single-climax shape "depended" - some games tense to the end, others had economy-gated down-phases. **Substantially met for Stack M; no rollback.**

title: Bodyguard Removal
body:
`[System: Bodyguard / Champion-Guard interaction]`
**What changes if the Bodyguard rule is removed entirely?**
- **Origin**: Session 25 brainstorm - designer asked "do we need the Bodyguard rule at all?" Bodyguard currently lets an adjacent Guard intercept a Move-Attack on a Champion/King. Without it, Champions become free Move-Attack targets for opposing Guards.
- **Why it matters**: Bodyguard is a chassis system. Per the Chassis/Engine lens, every chassis system should justify why the engine needs it. P3 and P4 evidence is mixed - Bodyguard *did* trigger organically in P3 (resolving OQ-21 favorably) but stayed at 0 triggers in P4 (correlated with the Armor-stall covariate). With Bodyguard absent, Champions would face direct Guard pressure - could make mid-game more active or could make Champions glass cannons.
- **Designer note**: explicitly low priority - "other questions here have more priority." Park as live OQ but do not bundle into the GLC change set unless it surfaces as a problem there.
- **Justification (per Rule)**: tests whether Bodyguard pays for its chassis volume (G4 cognitive load + rule explanation cost). If removal doesn't damage game-feel, the rule is dead weight.
- **Re-entry trigger**: standalone playtest after GLC stabilises. Or earlier if Bodyguard surfaces as a problem during GLC playtests.
- **Connected to**: OQ-21 (Bodyguard trigger watch - would close negatively if removal feels fine); Chassis/Engine lens (Bodyguard is pure chassis).

---

## Resolution (session-31, 2026-06-23)

**Withdrawn - no justification for removal.** Designer call: Bodyguard stays. The OQ was framed around testing whether removal feels fine, but per the Justification Rule, removing a rule requires a clear reason and we don't have one. P3 evidence (Bodyguard triggered organically, resolving OQ-21 favorably) is the load-bearing data point; P4's zero triggers correlate with the Armor-stall covariate, not with Bodyguard being inert. title: Skill-Phase action progression curve
body:
# Skill-Phase action progression curve

Stack M's body states:

> Skill Phase actions start at 2 per turn, scaling up over the game (matching the existing progression curve).

The Move Phase has a fixed 2 actions per turn. The Skill Phase budget is the variable. Stack M does not give explicit numbers for the curve - it says "matching the existing progression curve" but does not reproduce it.

## Required to ship Slice 5 / Slice 7

Engine needs to know, for each `round_number`, how many Skill-Phase actions the side-to-move receives. Until this is locked, the engine treats Skill-Phase actions as constant 2 - the same as Move Phase.

## Questions

1. What was the paper-baseline progression curve? (Archive: `archive/paper-pipeline/test-scenarios/`)
2. Does Stack M intend a literal copy of that curve, or does the +1-per-5-rounds income cadence imply the action cadence is similar?
3. Endpoint: cap at some N, or unbounded growth until game ends?

## Resolution path

Pull the paper baseline action-progression numbers from the archive, propose them as the Stack M default in the digital engine, and either commit (designer confirms) or open a follow-on stack that tunes the curve.

## Cross-refs

- `stack-m` (parent)
- `oq-66` (game length target - the curve is the primary lever)
- `principle-7` (bundled methodology - Stack M consciously did not relitigate this)

---

## Resolution (session-31, 2026-06-23)

The paper-baseline progression curve (`archive/paper-pipeline/test-scenarios/shared/baseline-sections.typ` line 370) is adopted into Stack M as written: **R1-10: 2, R11-20: 3, R21-30: 4, R31+: 5, …** - **unbounded**, +1 action per 10 rounds. The "R31+: 5" line in the paper rule sheet was shorthand for the table cut-off, NOT a cap; R41+: 6, R51+: 7, and so on.

Engine implementation: `game/crates/core_engine/src/game_logic/make_unmake.rs::skill_phase_budget(round_number) -> u8 = 2 + (round_number - 1) / 10`. Wired into `apply_end_phase` (Move → Skill transition). Symmetric helper `income_per_turn` lives in `turn_manager.rs` for the parallel income curve (`2 + round_number / 5`, also unbounded). Both have unit-test coverage including the past-31 / past-cutoff cases.

The question is now *volume*, not *balance* - does the Armor↔Armor-Breaker loop draw attention away from the combo loop both players are trying to discover (Framing B)?

title: Draft Entry Complexity + Skill Permanence
body:
`[System: Skill Drafting] [Affects: New player onboarding, Mid-game adaptability]`
**Three linked problems**:
- **A - Draft entry complexity**: New players cannot evaluate skills during draft (no on-board experience). Compounded by catalogue size: more skills = more options to evaluate before the first move.
- **B - Permanent draft decisions**: Mid-game realisation that loadout doesn't fit board state, no way to adapt.
- **C - In-game reference load**: Two compounding sources.
  - *C1 - Lookup friction (UX layer)*: Constant board↔skill-list switching. Physical skill cards on the table reduce this directly.
  - *C2 - Skill identity volume (structural layer)*: Number of distinct skills a player must mentally model - own loadout + opponent's loadout. UX fixes do NOT address this. More skills equipped per side = more identities to track. Currently ~8 identities at the table (4 Champions × 2 slots × 2 players).
- **Tension with OQ-12 (catalogue expansion to ~25)**: Catalogue size primarily affects A (more options to evaluate at draft), not C2 (capped by equipped-slot count). But a larger catalogue still makes the draft harder for new players. Expansion and onboarding need to be reconciled.
- **Design constraint**: Solution must not reduce strategic depth for experienced players.
- **Solution candidates**:
  - For A: try-before-lock draft phase; simplified starter loadouts (skip draft on first game); tiered "core vs. advanced" skill catalogue (new players play core-only).
  - For B: in-game skill switching; mid-game redraft event.
  - For C1: physical skill cards (low-risk UX fix). **SHIPPED Session 18** (`shared/skill-cards.pdf`).
  - For C2: lower equipped-slot count (Stack D / OQ-27 territory); force loadout overlap (smaller draft pool, duplicates across Champions); tiered catalogue (also helps A).
- **P4 evidence (`docs/research/playtest-4-analysis.md`)**:
  - A1: "easy to understand, strategy not easy though" - rules clear, depth not surface-readable on turn 1.
  - C7 (lookup frequency): "rather often, just for the details, felt okay (1st game)" - physical skill cards helped (Q-C1 UX layer working).
  - **Q-D1 reading: contaminated.** Elias did NOT honour the teacher-vocab-checklist commitment. Wrote: *"I just used the words to make it clear what the game is about"* + pitch box noted he "explained a lot of my experience and good combos." Niko's engine vocabulary ("combinations", "skill combos", "stacking of skills") cannot be cleanly attributed to game experience - much of it could be borrowed.
  - D14: **Same puzzle** (highest Framing-B signal - but contamination flag applies).
  - D11 mixed engine + chassis vocabulary; E15: "chess, deckbuilding."
- **Verdict**: Q-D1 ≥2/4 strong-signal threshold NOT met by this session. Need ≥1 more first-timer session with proper vocab discipline before Framing B can be evaluated.

title: Focus on Move-skills - player-choice modelling
body:
# Focus on Move-skills - player-choice modelling

Stack M's Skill Reference for Focus reads:

> Focus (cost 1, Mystic): The next skill used by any of your pieces this turn gains +1 Range. **Move skills: caster chooses activation-range or effect-range, not both.**

The sentence after the bold-equivalent is a per-Move-skill choice: when Focus is active and the next skill is a Move skill (Dash, Blast, Shove, Hook's pull, Swap, Retreat, Tempest's push), the caster must pick one of two interpretations of the +1 Range buff:

1. **Activation-range** - the buff extends *who can be targeted*. E.g. Shove (Range 2) can now affect a Range-3 target.
2. **Effect-range** - the buff extends *how far the effect reaches*. E.g. Shove (push 1 tile) now pushes 2 tiles.

Not both at once.

## Engine implications

Action encoding needs to express this choice. Options:

- **(A)** Add a per-skill `choice_idx` bit that means "Focus interpretation = activation/effect". Reuses the existing 4-bit field; collides with the existing `choice_idx` uses (Shove direction, Retreat Guard-pick) so requires careful per-skill semantics.
- **(B)** Treat Focus consumption as two distinct skill IDs at draft-time (Focus-A and Focus-E). Ugly and changes the skill table.
- **(C)** Make Focus pop up a sub-choice in `make()` and require the caller to encode it in the action's `choice_idx` reserved bits.

(A) is leanest. Lock at Slice 4 (skill resolver) - does not block Slice 1 (Move Phase only).

## Questions

1. Is the activation-vs-effect choice always offered, even if only one is mechanically meaningful?
2. Does the choice happen at *activation* time (player declares), or at *target* time (player picks a target and the engine infers)?

## Cross-refs

- `stack-m` (parent)
- `oq-69` (sibling - both block Slice 5/4 deliverables)
- `principle-core-fantasy` (Focus is the spell-combo enabler)

---

## Resolution (session-31, 2026-06-23)

**Not a design question - an engine implementation detail.** Stack M's rule is unambiguous: when Focus is active and the next skill is a Move skill, the caster chooses activation-range OR effect-range, not both. The engine generator handles this by enumerating BOTH branches as separate legal actions per Move-skill cast when Focus is pending: one action with the buff applied to activation-range, one with it applied to effect-range. The choice is encoded in the action itself; the search tree picks between them like any other branching decision.

No new sub-choice mechanism in `make()`, no extra Focus skill IDs, no semantic collision with existing `choice_idx` uses needed - the choice is materialised as separate enumerated actions at generator time, which is the canonical way the engine handles all player choices.

Slice 6 (Focus wiring) implements this by:
- `apply_focus` sets a `pending_modifiers::FOCUS` bit (single bit - no activation/effect distinction stored).
- When the next skill is a Move skill, the generator emits two distinct actions for each legal target - one tagged "Focus buffs activation", one tagged "Focus buffs effect". The Move-skill resolver reads the tag and applies the buff to the right dimension.
- When the next skill is a non-Move skill (Strike/Shield/Mystic), the generator emits only one action per target with the +1 Range applied to activation-range (no choice to make).

## Addendum (session-31, 2026-06-23) - Self-only retargeting

A second clarification surfaced during Slice 6 implementation: Focus on **Self-only skills** (Shield, Dash, Retreat) does not just buff range - it permits **channelling the skill onto an adjacent ally** as an alternative interpretation. Concretely:

- **Shield + Focus** → +1 Armor on the caster *or* on an adjacent ally.
- **Dash + Focus** → caster moves up to 4 tiles *or* an adjacent ally moves up to 2.
- **Retreat + Focus** → caster retreats at Range+1 *or* an adjacent ally retreats (to a square adjacent to a friendly Guard; same effect, different recipient).

Engine implementation: the Action encoding gains a new `aux_sq` field (bits 23..29, with a `has_aux` bit at 29). When set, the resolver applies the effect to `aux_sq` instead of `src`. The generator emits these retarget actions as additional legal branches whenever Focus is pending and the caster has an eligible adjacent ally.

## Addendum (session-31) - Charge / Focus stacking constraints

- **Charge text** changed to "the next *Strike* skill" (was "one Strike skill ... this turn"). Functionally the same in nearly all positions, but precise: Charge waits for *one specific* Strike skill (the next), then is consumed.
- **Focus text** changed to "the next *non-Mystic* skill". Casting Focus → Charge → Strike applies both buffs; casting Charge → Focus → Strike does the same (order of buffs does not matter for Strike outcome). Focus → Focus and Charge → Charge are **illegal** (max 1 of each active at a time). The generator filters duplicates; the resolver debug-asserts as defence-in-depth.

title: Shield / Plate cast on a piece at the Armor cap
body:
## Question

What happens when Shield (self) or Plate (adjacent ally) is cast on a target already at the Armor cap (2 in Stack M)? Three options: (a) silent no-op (cast still consumes money/action), (b) illegal cast (generator filters), (c) overflow / wraparound.

## Resolution

**Illegal cast (b).** The generator filters Shield in `SelfOnly` and Plate in `Ally` branches when the target's armor is already `>= ARMOR_CAP`. Resolvers carry `debug_assert!(prev.armor() < ARMOR_CAP)` guards but no recovery logic.

Contrast: Break against a 0-armor target is legal - it doesn't produce the "no effect" feel because Break's purpose includes ticking the combo counter (and Break under Charge still deals 1 HP damage). Buff skills with no orthogonal payoff at cap are pure dead-weight casts → filtered.

Implementation:
- `generator.rs::generate_skill_phase` - `SelfOnly` arm filters Shield at cap; `Ally` arm filters Plate at cap.
- `make_unmake.rs::apply_shield` / `apply_plate` - `debug_assert!(prev.armor() < ARMOR_CAP)`.

title: Heal cast on a non-Injured ally
body:
## Question

What happens when Heal is cast on an ally who is already at full HP? Same three options as the armor-cap question.

## Resolution

**Illegal cast.** The generator filters Heal in the `Ally` branch when `tgt.hp() != INJURED_HP` (1). Heal has no orthogonal payoff (no combo tick on allies, no other rider) so a no-op cast would just be wasted action/money.

Implementation:
- `generator.rs::generate_skill_phase` - `Ally` arm match-arm on `Skill::Heal` continues when target HP != 1.
- `make_unmake.rs::apply_heal` - `debug_assert!(prev.hp() == INJURED_HP)`.

title: All movement skills must actually relocate
body:
## Question

Should a zero-movement cast - Dash with dest=src, Swap with target=caster, Retreat with dest=src - be legal? E.g. "I cast Dash but stay put to spend the action."

## Resolution

**Illegal at generator time** for every movement skill. The generator never emits a movement-skill action whose dest equals src (Dash, Retreat) or whose target equals caster (Swap). `magic::skill_attacks` already excludes src by construction; `path::skill_targets` also excludes src; so the constraint holds "for free" with no extra filter needed in the generator code path.

Reason given by the designer: a zero-move movement skill is "stupid as fuck" - there's no game-design payoff and it's a degenerate option that bloats the legal-action list.

Implementation: structural - falls out of `skill_attacks` / `skill_targets` semantics. Resolvers carry `debug_assert!(src != dest)` guards.

title: Swap target ownership: ally only, or ally + enemy?
body:
## Question

Stack-M's combo-rule body says "Multi-Champion combo ticks on movement-causing skills, including Swap when it relocates an enemy." Does that imply Swap can target an enemy?

## Resolution

**Ally only.** Swap is positional repositioning between two friendly pieces (caster + allied target). The Stack-M body phrasing about "Swap when it relocates an enemy" is theoretical / forward-looking - Stack-M itself does not implement enemy-target Swap, and no playtest data motivates adding it. Locking it down to ally-only also keeps the apply_swap resolver simple (no combo-tick branch, no ownership-mismatch bitboard updates).

If a future stack revives enemy-target Swap, the generator's `Ally` arm widens to `Either` and apply_swap gains a combo-tick branch + cross-side bitboard XOR.

Implementation:
- `generator.rs::generate_skill_phase` - Swap's TargetOwner is `Ally`, so the `Ally` arm filters to `raw & stm_bb`.
- `make_unmake.rs::apply_swap` - assumes same-side ownership; only kind-layer bitboards are XORed.

title: Combo counter on friendly-piece pushes
body:
## Question

When a Shove (or any future friendly-push skill) pushes an allied piece, does it tick the multi-Champion combo counter?

## Resolution

**No - friendly-piece pushes never tick combo.** Stack-M body is explicit: "What doesn't count: ... Pushing a friendly piece." Implemented as an enemy-check gate in `apply_shove`: combo_tick + pre-tick combo bonus damage only fire when the target is on the opposing side.

This keeps Shove as a tactical repositioning tool when used on allies - no "stack combo on my own pieces for later free damage" exploit.

Implementation: `make_unmake.rs::apply_shove` - `if target_is_enemy { combo_tick(...); pre-tick combo bonus damage }` ; the push itself fires regardless of ownership.

title: Skill movement geometry - queen-ray vs. king-zigzag
body:
## Question

Move-Phase plain moves are king-style (any 8-direction path, intermediate squares must be empty, Chebyshev distance ≤ speed). Should skill-driven movement (Dash, Retreat, Hook's pull, Blast/Shove's push, Tempest's push, Swap) follow the same king-zigzag geometry or a different rule?

## Resolution

**Queen-ray straight line only.** All skill movement happens along the 8 queen-rays (N/NE/E/SE/S/SW/W/NW) - no zigzag, no intermediate direction changes. The Path/Range/Block primitive (`magic::skill_attacks`) already enforces this for target enumeration; movement skills land on a square that is on a single ray from the caster within the skill's range, with no intermediate occupancy.

Designer rationale: skill movement is a *skill* - distinct from the basic movement you'd expect from any piece. The king has 1 speed like any other Champion; "king-style zigzag" only describes Move-Phase plain moves, which are unrelated to skill effects.

Implementation: structural - Dash/Retreat use `magic::skill_attacks(...) & !occ`; Hook/Blast/Tempest/Swap use `path::skill_targets` for target picking and `magic::step_toward` / `step_away` / `neighbour_in_dir` for the actual relocation, all of which are queen-ray operations.

title: tracked_enemies OOB in make_unmake during time-bounded gauntlet matches
body:
## Status: resolved (session-37, engine fix)

## Symptom
`make_unmake.rs:979` - `tracked_enemies` array overflow when more than `MAX_TRACKED_ENEMIES=8` distinct combo-tick targets are touched in a single turn. Debug builds caught it via `debug_assert!`; release builds stripped the assert and proceeded to UB. Surfaced by the gauntlet's real-match tests in `nn_trainer/src/gauntlet.rs`.

## Root cause
`apply_tempest` called `combo_tick` on **every** occupied neighbour it relocated - friend or foe - while Stack M's combo rule places counters on **enemies only**, and the `MAX_TRACKED_ENEMIES=8` cap was sized for enemies-only (also constrained by the u64 packing in `champion_credit`: `caster_slot * 8 + target_slot`). Ticking friendlies pushed slot consumption to ~13 (≤7 own + ≤6 enemy) and tripped the cap.

The other movement skills (Shove, Blast, Hook) already enemy-gated their `combo_tick` calls. Tempest was the outlier.

## Fix (session-37)
1. **Engine:** `apply_tempest` now computes `caster_is_p1` once and only calls `combo_tick` when the neighbour is on the opposing side. Friendly pieces are still relocated; they just don't tick. Mirrors the `target_is_enemy` gate in `apply_shove`.
2. **Safety net:** `ensure_tracked_enemy` / `ensure_tracked_caster` now use `assert!` instead of `debug_assert!`, so any future cap overflow panics loudly in release rather than UB-ing past the array.

## Lessons
- The Stack M doc was the spec, not the engine. The previous session's reconciliation (which flipped this) was based on a misread of the cap's structural role - fixed in this resolution.
- `debug_assert!` guarding an unchecked array write is unsafe in release. Audit other `debug_assert!` sites that gate writes.

title: Tempest AOE combo-tick policy
body:
## Question

When Tempest pushes adjacent pieces, does the combo counter tick on:
(a) only the target,
(b) target + each pushed neighbour (strict Stack-M reading), or
(c) some other policy?

Stack-M says combo ticks when a Strike or movement-causing skill *affects* a piece by a new Champion. Tempest is movement-causing for the pushed neighbours, so the strict reading is (b).

## Resolution

**Strict reading (b)** - target + each pushed neighbour ticks. Encoded in apply_tempest: combo_tick fires for the target via apply_strike_damage, then again on each pushed neighbour just before relocate_piece. Same-caster-same-turn dedup is enforced via champion_credit, so a Tempest cannot re-tick the same neighbour twice.

Implementation: game/crates/core_engine/src/game_logic/make_unmake.rs::apply_tempest.

title: Push off-board behaviour for movement-causing skills
body:
## Question

When a movement-causing skill (Tempest AOE push, Shove, Blast, etc.) would push a piece off the board, what happens?

Options:
(a) Push fails - piece stays put, no other effect.
(b) Push succeeds - piece is removed from the board (off-board = death).
(c) Push partially resolves - piece stays put but combo still ticks / other side-effects apply.

## Resolution

**(a) Push fails - piece stays put.** No removal, no combo-tick on a piece whose push fails (the strict-policy combo-tick precedes the push in apply_tempest, so for off-board cases the tick effectively does not happen because step_away returns None and the resolver s before combo_tick).

Rationale: removing pieces by *schubsen* gives push-skills a hidden one-shot kill mode that Stack-M does not intend. Failing keeps push purely positional.

Implementation: game/crates/core_engine/src/state/magic.rs::step_away returns None when target rank/file would fall outside [0,8). game_logic/make_unmake.rs::apply_tempest skips the entire pushed-neighbour iteration when step_away is None.

title: Blast vs. Shove off-board push asymmetry
body:
## Question

Blast and Shove both push an enemy 1 tile. When the push would leave the board, what happens? Should both be filtered at generation time, or both fizzle silently in the resolver?

## Resolution

**Asymmetric.**

- **Shove** is pre-filtered at the generator: an off-board push (or push into an occupied square) is never emitted. Reason: Shove is a *pure movement* skill - if the push fails, the cast accomplishes nothing, which is purposeless and (per the broader "all movement skills must actually relocate" rule) illegal.
- **Blast** fizzles silently in the resolver. Reason: Blast is the *push category* skill - even if the push fails, other riders (combo tick, pre-tick combo bonus damage) still fire. The push fizzling silently keeps those riders live without separate-rule duplication. (For Stack-M as written, Blast has no damage rider - just push and combo-tick - but the pattern is reusable if future tuning adds one.)

Both are valid encodings of the "movement skill that landed somewhere illegal" geometry; the difference is whether there's an orthogonal payoff that justifies casting anyway.

Implementation:
- `generator.rs::generate_skill_phase` - `Either` arm (Shove) skips dirs where `neighbour_in_dir` returns None or the push square is occupied.
- `make_unmake.rs::apply_blast` - wraps push in `if let Some(push_dest) = magic::step_away(src, tgt) { if !pos.is_occupied(push_dest) { relocate_piece(...) } }`.

title: Retreat with no allied Guards on the board
body:
## Question

Retreat's legality requires that the destination square is adjacent to a friendly Guard. If the side-to-move has zero Guards left, Retreat has no legal destinations - should the generator silently emit nothing, or should we explicitly flag it as "no Retreat available"?

## Resolution

**Generator filters at the per-caster level** - if `stm_bb & guards == 0`, the Retreat branch continues without emitting any action. There's no game-state flag or panic; the resolver also assumes destinations are valid (`debug_assert` on relocation). Behaves identically to any other "no legal target" case.

Implementation: `generator.rs::generate_skill_phase` - Empty arm, `Skill::Retreat` branch, `if ally_guards == 0 { continue; }`.

title: AI search: branching factor profile + search-strategy plan
body:
# AI search: branching factor profile + search-strategy plan

The engine generator emits **atomic legal actions one at a time** (one move, one skill cast, or `EndPhase`), not full-turn commitments. The search tree therefore layers naturally - one ply per atomic action, with phase transitions (`EndPhase`) acting as ordinary plies. This already keeps any single node's branching factor finite, but Stack M still has substantial per-node fan-out that any AI opponent must mitigate.

## Two layers to this OQ

### Layer 1 - Measurement (empirical, needs the engine running)

Once Slice 6 lands and we can simulate full games, profile:
- Mean and worst-case legal-action count per ply in **Move Phase** (per-piece × reachable squares, post-Bodyguard filtering).
- Mean and worst-case legal-action count per ply in **Skill Phase**, broken down by round bucket - Skill-Phase budget grows over time (2/3/4/5+) so late-game branching compounds.
- How Focus and Charge multiply the count (each piece can buff first, then strike - the *sequence* matters).
- Combo-counter state contribution (every enemy-with-combo target is a damage vector for every movement skill - late-game combo state explodes target counts for non-Strike skills too).

Outcome: a table or chart showing per-ply branching distribution across game phases and round buckets. Until we have this, all search-strategy choices are guesswork.

### Layer 2 - Strategy (downstream of measurement)

Standard alpha-beta-family mitigations, in rough order of cost-to-implement vs payoff:

1. **Move ordering** - sort actions by static heuristic (captures first, threats, then quiet). Massive alpha-beta speedup; no correctness impact. Cheap.
2. **Transposition table** - Zobrist hashing is already on the Slice 6 TODO list (populate `undo.zobrist_xor`). TT becomes viable as soon as that lands.
3. **Killer-move heuristic** + **history heuristic** - standard, cheap, well-understood.
4. **Iterative deepening** with phase awareness - Stack M's phases are strict; we can search one phase at a time and use intermediate eval at phase boundaries to prune deeper.
5. **Symmetry reduction** - the board has reflection symmetry; can prune mirror lines in opening.
6. **Quiescence search** - extend search past Strike-skill chains so the engine doesn't bail mid-combo and mis-evaluate.

## Why this matters now

Engine wiring is up through Slice 5; AI opponent work is not yet on the roadmap, but it will be - `next_steps` priority 10 mentions digital-prototype tooling, and the digital-first pivot (Session 27) implicitly requires a playable AI for self-play testing. This OQ is tracked now so that **Slice 6+ implementation choices** (Zobrist, end-of-turn hashing, action encoding) are made with eventual search in mind, not retrofitted later.

## What this OQ does NOT cover

- The choice of search algorithm itself (alpha-beta vs MCTS vs hybrid). That's ADR-territory, not OQ-territory - open it as an ADR once Layer 1 measurements are in.
- Position evaluation function design (material, king safety, combo-counter pressure, skill-economy state, etc.). That's a separate concern from search-tree shape.

## Cross-refs

- `oq-69` (Skill-Phase action curve - resolved session-31; informs late-game branching profile).
- `next_steps` priority 10 (digital prototype persistence - search needs persistent positions).
- Stack M body (`stacks.id = 'stack-m'`) - the ruleset whose branching is being characterised.
- `adr-005` (digital architecture - the engine this AI will plug into).

## Resolution path

1. Slice 6 lands → engine can play full games end-to-end.
2. Write a profiling harness that walks legal actions at every ply of self-play games (random or naive policy is fine for measurement).
3. Collect Layer 1 data; commit a table to the OQ body.
4. Open ADR for search-algorithm choice with Layer 1 data as input.
5. Resolve this OQ when both layers are addressed (data + adopted mitigations).

title: Retreat effect-mode: land 2 tiles from a Guard?
body:
# Retreat effect-mode: land 2 tiles from a Guard?

Stack M Retreat reads: "Self: move along the Path to land **adjacent to** one of your Guards." With Focus active, the player picks activation-range or effect-range:

- **Activation interpretation** is clear: Range becomes 4 (default 3 + 1), so longer-distance retreats are reachable.
- **Effect interpretation** is *Stack M-silent*. Designer floated (session-31) the idea that Focus-effect-Retreat could **relax the landing constraint** - land 1 *or* 2 tiles away from a Guard. Currently NOT implemented; the engine treats Retreat as activation-range-only when Focus is active (matches the un-Focused rule).

## Why this exists separately

Focus on Move-skills (Dash/Blast/Shove) has a clean activation/effect distinction. Retreat is awkward: its "effect" is more like a *target predicate* (which empty squares are legal) than a quantity to extend. "Land 2 from a Guard" is the most natural read but the rule sheet does not state it.

## Resolution path

Either:
- **(A)** Adopt "land ≤2 from a Guard with Focus-effect" - engine adds a retarget-style branch, generator emits it.
- **(B)** Keep effect-mode unimplemented for Retreat - Focus on Retreat is always activation-mode. Document in Stack M.
- **(C)** Replace Retreat-effect with an entirely different mechanic (e.g. "carry an adjacent ally to the landing square") - out of scope unless playtest demands it.

## Cross-refs

- `stack-m` (parent)
- `oq-70` (sibling - Focus on Move-skills, where the choice originally surfaced)

title: AI draft strategy - replace fixed-preset stand-in with real search/heuristic
body:
## Context

L8 Phase C (Session 33, 2026-06-25) ships AI draft behaviour as a **placeholder**: when `step_ai` is invoked in `Phase::Draft`, the engine drives the AI side through a hardcoded pre-made loadout - playing the next 2 picks of that loadout per ply until draft completes. This means AI seats never actually "choose" during draft; they just unroll a fixed deck.

This is intentional for the L8 slice. The user explicitly rejected random picks (junk loadouts would regress AIvAI playtest signal vs. today's makeshift preset); option 1 (fixed preset) was chosen over option 2 (greedy heuristic) and option 3 (real draft-tree search) to keep the L8 surface small and not pretend to be smarter than it is.

## What needs to happen

Replace the fixed-preset stand-in in `core_engine::search::ai_draft_turn` (or wherever the Phase C wiring lands - file path to confirm during the follow-up slice) with a real AI draft strategy. Likely shape:

1. **Heuristic baseline** - score candidate `(skill, sq, slot)` triples per pick (e.g. don't double Mystic on one piece, King favours defensive skills, Champions near front rank favour aggressive ones). Cheap to run, plausible play.
2. **Draft-tree search** - proper expectimax/minimax over draft moves. The branching factor at draft start is large (~30k DraftTurns), so this likely needs domain-specific pruning (pick-set first, slot assignment second) before search becomes viable.
3. **Loadout evaluator** - at terminal draft state (Phase::Move, both sides fully equipped), the regular `evaluate()` function gives a static score. The search backs that up the draft tree. Question: is `evaluate()` accurate enough on a freshly-equipped position with no movement history? May need a draft-specific evaluator.

## Related

- oq-81 (AI search: branching factor profile + search-strategy plan) - same family of search-tuning question, draft branching profile probably belongs in the same data set.
- L8 Phase C - landed the placeholder this OQ replaces.
- oq-62 (Draft information / simultaneous vs sequential reveal) - resolved to sequential alternating, so the search tree is per-side-to-move with full info, no hidden-info subgame.

## Acceptance

- AI draft no longer relies on a fixed preset; picks reflect heuristic and/or search.
- AIvAI smoke tests (`aivai_demo` with `--show-board`) produce loadouts that are not literally identical run-to-run.
- Search time stays within the AI budget (default 200ms/ply) - if draft search is meaningfully slower than play-phase search, document that and consider a separate `draft_time_limit_ms` budget on `AiBudget`.

title: Greying-out semantics when bodyguard intercepts a Move-Attack
body:
## Context

Stack M Move-Attack with bodyguard interception: attacker piece moves toward `target`, but a defender-adjacent Guard intercepts, so the attacker's final square is the bodyguard's slot (`approach` adjacent to original target), not the original target. Today the UI marks the attacker's `finalSq` as "used this phase" regardless of whether interception happened.

## Question

Two design positions:

- **(A) "Used = the piece moved this phase, regardless of intercept."** Current behaviour. Justification: the piece spent its action; nothing more it can do this Move phase. Simple, predictable.
- **(B) "Used = the piece reached the *intended* target."** If a bodyguard intercepts, the attacker's attack was *partially* spent (movement happened but the kill resolved elsewhere). Open question whether the piece should be free to act again or not.

## Why this is a design question, not a bug

The L7c parity fix (session 33) ensured both peers see the *same* greyed-out state. Whether that state is the right semantics is the open question.

## Sequencing

Low urgency - no playtest depends on this yet. Resolve before the next Stack M digital playtest if Move-Attack + Bodyguard interactions show up frequently.

## Cross-refs

OQ-21 (Bodyguard Rule, critical). Stack M (Move-Attack rules).

title: Compensate the player who loses a piece with Money?
body:
`[System: Resource Economy] [Affects: Combat tempo, first-mover-loses standoff]`

**Should losing a piece grant the victim some Money?** Raised in P6 (Dorian playtest) as a design idea, not a UI feature - the designer explicitly wants the design side to ponder it, not just build it.

**What problem it might fix:** the P6 "first-mover-loses" standoff (oq-58) - whoever breaks a standoff loses a piece on the trade, so both sides wait for economy to rebuild. A losing-a-piece rebate would (a) soften the trade disadvantage that makes committing first punishing, and (b) give the down-material player a comeback lever, keeping games two-sided.

**Why it needs design scrutiny (not auto-accept):**
- **Distinct from bp-action-based-money-economy / oq-47.** Those reward the player who DEALS damage/captures (rewards the aggressor, snowball risk). This rewards the VICTIM - an anti-snowball / rubber-band mechanic. Opposite sign, different game-feel.
- **Perfect-info / no-luck constraint holds** (deterministic payout), so it doesn't violate a hard constraint, but rubber-banding can flatten the skill gradient - the thing that made P4-era performance-income (oq-47) get closed. Need to check it doesn't just reward losing.
- **Interacts with Focus-cost nerf (ns-32) and the first-mover lever (ns-34)** - may be redundant with, or compound, those. Should be weighed as one option among the oq-58 tempo levers, not adopted in isolation.
- **MDA:** mechanic = victim rebate; dynamic = players more willing to commit to trades / down-player stays in it; aesthetic = fewer dead standoffs, more back-and-forth. Justification Rule: fixes the oq-58 standoff, at the risk of dampening the reward for winning exchanges.

**Open sub-questions:** flat amount or scaled by piece value (Champion vs Guard vs King)? Does it apply to King capture (moot - game ends)? Only on skill-kills or also move-attack kills?

Source: P6 Dorian notes (session-42). Connected to: oq-58 (first-mover-loses standoff), oq-47 (performance-based income - closed), bp-action-based-money-economy (aggressor-reward counterpart), ns-32, ns-34.
